bullets: He returned to the front and was **killed on 4 November 1918**, one week before the Armistice. Most of his poems, including Exposure, were published after his death (1920).
His Preface says his subject is ‘War, and the pity of War’: he wanted to show the truth, against propaganda.
He experimented with **pararhyme** (half-rhyme with matching consonants), which became his signature.
He had worked for a vicar before the war and his faith was shaken by what he saw: hence stanza 7.
Contrast with Tennyson: Tennyson read about war in newspapers; Owen lived it.

callouts.p: Owen’s own winter of 1917 in the trenches explains why the weather, not the enemy, is the main threat. Tie this to the personification of the wind and dawn.

core.h: Context (AO3): Owen and the Western Front
core.p: Wilfred Owen (1893–1918) enlisted in 1915 and served as an officer on the **Western Front**. In early 1917 he experienced the bitter winter in the trenches (one of the coldest on record), where many men died of **hypothermia and frostbite**. Diagnosed with shell shock, he was treated at **Craiglockhart Hospital** in Edinburgh, where he met Siegfried Sassoon, who encouraged his anti-war poetry.

bullets: **Conflict type**: men vs nature; the futility of war; inner conflict of faith.
**Big message**: war is not glorious action but endless suffering and waiting; nature is indifferent and lethal.
**Perspective**: first-person plural ‘we’, present tense: immediate and shared.
core.p: Soldiers in a trench at night cannot sleep because of the freezing wind and the silence. They watch, wait, and hear distant guns, but no attack comes. Dawn brings only more misery. Snow is deadlier than the occasional bullets. Drowsy with cold, they dream of home but imagine its doors closed to them. They try to justify dying to protect home and faith, but feel that God’s love is dying. In the last stanza the frost kills men and a burying party finds frozen faces. Nothing happens.

bullets: **Pararhyme** creates a sense of something wrong, incomplete, unresolved, like the soldiers’ lives.
Long lines with ellipses slow the pace: monotony and exhaustion.

The **refrain** variations track despair: ‘But nothing happens’ → ‘What are we doing here?’ → ‘Is it that we are dying?’ → ‘We turn back to our dying’ → ‘For love of God seems dying’ → ‘But nothing happens’.
**Cyclical structure**: beginning and end are the same; time passes but nothing changes.
Present tense and ‘we’ make the reader share the experience.
core.p: Eight stanzas of five lines: four long lines and a short **half-line refrain**. The rhyme scheme is **ABBAC**, but almost all rhymes are **pararhymes** (wire/war, brambles/rumbles, grow/grey).

plan: Structures of repetition: refrain vs question-and-answer
essays.q: Compare how the futility of war is presented in Exposure and What Were They Like?
essays.text: Owen builds futility into the structure of Exposure. Each stanza ends with a short half-line, and the refrain ‘But nothing happens’ returns at the start, the middle and the end, so the poem itself goes nowhere, just as the soldiers wait through a night and a dawn that bring only ‘misery’. Even the climactic death in the final stanza, where the burying party finds that ‘All their eyes are ice’, is followed by the same flat refrain: mass death has changed nothing. Levertov also uses a rigid structure to show futility, but in a different way: her poem is built from a set of questions about the Vietnamese people, each answered in turn, and the formal, numbered answers emphasise how completely the war has destroyed the culture they ask about. While Owen’s soldiers dream of a home whose ‘doors are closed’ to them, Levertov’s answers suggest an entire way of life closed off by bombing. Writing as a soldier in 1917, Owen protests against the waste of his own generation; writing in the 1960s as an American opponent of the Vietnam War, Levertov protests against the destruction her own country caused to others. Both end in silence: Owen’s men freeze while ‘nothing happens’, and Levertov’s speaker concludes that no one can now know the answers.
essays.thesis: Both poems present war as pointless destruction, but Owen shows futility from inside the soldiers’ experience, through inaction and repetition, while Levertov shows it from outside, through the erasure of a whole culture that can no longer be remembered.
why: Compares structure first, which is the most perceptive route here.
AO3 for both poets linked to their protest purposes.
Refers to Levertov’s features without reproducing her lines (copyright).

poem.how: Each stanza ends with a short half-line: notice how those half-lines change.

stanzas.label: Stanza 1
lines: Our brains ache, in the merciless iced east winds that knive us . . .
Wearied we keep awake because the night is silent . . .
Low, drooping flares confuse our memory of the salient . . .
Worried by silence, sentries whisper, curious, nervous,
But nothing happens.

notes.n: Opens with **collective first person** ‘Our’: Owen speaks for all the soldiers. Pain is mental as well as physical.
**Personification**: the wind is ‘merciless’, a cruel enemy. **Sibilance** (iced, east, winds) creates a hissing, biting sound.
Noun turned into a verb: the wind stabs like a blade. Nature becomes a weapon.
**Ellipses** at the end of lines slow the pace and suggest endless waiting, time dragging.
Military term: a section of the front line jutting into enemy territory. Shows Owen’s first-hand experience.
Sibilance and a list of adjectives build tension; ‘curious, nervous’ is a **pararhyme** pair.
The **refrain**: anticlimax. The half-line is short and flat, like a deflated sigh. Futility and boredom are central to the soldiers’ experience.

stanzas.label: Stanza 2
lines: Watching, we hear the mad gusts tugging on the wire,
Like twitching agonies of men among its brambles.
Northward, incessantly, the flickering gunnery rumbles,
Far off, like a dull rumour of some other war.
What are we doing here?

notes.n: The wind is personified as ‘mad’, insane. Barbed wire was the deadliest feature of no man’s land.
Disturbing **simile**: the wind-shaken wire looks like dying men caught on it, which was a real sight. ‘Brambles’ turns wire into a cruel natural plant.
notes.w: Like twitching agonies of men among its brambles.

notes.n: **Pararhyme** (half-rhyme) with ‘war’ in line 4: the near-rhymes are unsettling and never quite resolve, like the soldiers’ situation.
**Onomatopoeia** (‘rumbles’) and **assonance**; the real fighting is distant, ‘incessantly’ in the background.
notes.w: Northward, incessantly, the flickering gunnery rumbles,

notes.n: The refrain changes to a **rhetorical question**: the soldiers question the whole purpose of the war. Owen’s anti-war voice.

stanzas.label: Stanza 3
lines: The poignant misery of dawn begins to grow . . .
We only know war lasts, rain soaks, and clouds sag stormy.
Dawn massing in the east her melancholy army
Attacks once more in ranks on shivering ranks of grey,
But nothing happens.

notes.n: Dawn usually symbolises hope and new life; here it brings only misery. **Subverts** a traditional image.
**Tricolon** of short, blunt clauses: the only certainties are suffering. Monotonous rhythm.
notes.w: We only know war lasts, rain soaks, and clouds sag stormy.

notes.n: **Extended metaphor**: dawn is an enemy army, attacking the soldiers. Nature, not the Germans, is the real enemy.
notes.w: Dawn massing in the east her melancholy army

notes.n: Ambiguous: grey clouds, grey German uniforms, or the grey, cold British soldiers themselves. Repetition of ‘ranks’ suggests endless waves.

stanzas.label: Stanza 4
lines: Sudden successive flights of bullets streak the silence.
Less deadly than the air that shudders black with snow,
With sidelong flowing flakes that flock, pause, and renew,
We watch them wandering up and down the wind's nonchalance,
But nothing happens.

notes.n: **Sibilance** imitates the hiss of bullets. The only human attack in the poem, and it is brief.
notes.w: Sudden successive flights of bullets streak the silence.

notes.n: The key claim of the poem: the **weather is deadlier than the enemy’s bullets**.
**Alliteration** of soft ‘f’ sounds and the delicate snowflakes contrast with their deadly effect. The **caesuras** mimic the flakes’ stop-start motion.
notes.w: sidelong flowing flakes that flock, pause, and renew,

notes.n: Nature is **indifferent**: it does not care whether men live or die.

stanzas.label: Stanza 5
lines: Pale flakes with fingering stealth come feeling for our faces—
We cringe in holes, back on forgotten dreams, and stare, snow-dazed,
Deep into grassier ditches. So we drowse, sun-dozed,
Littered with blossoms trickling where the blackbird fusses.
—Is it that we are dying?

notes.n: Sinister **personification** with alliterative ‘f’: the snow creeps like a thief or a ghost, searching for victims.
notes.w: Pale flakes with fingering stealth come feeling for our faces—

notes.n: Animal-like, humiliated: men reduced to hiding in holes.
Hypothermia: the men drift into dreams. ‘Snow-dazed’ vs ‘sun-dozed’ shows the shift from reality to memory.
**Pastoral imagery** of an English summer: the warm memories of home contrast with the frozen trenches.
notes.w: Littered with blossoms trickling where the blackbird fusses.

notes.n: The refrain becomes a terrified question. The **dash** shows a sudden break as they realise the dreaminess may be death from cold.

stanzas.label: Stanza 6
lines: Slowly our ghosts drag home: glimpsing the sunk fires, glozed
With crusted dark-red jewels; crickets jingle there;
For hours the innocent mice rejoice: the house is theirs;
Shutters and doors, all closed: on us the doors are closed,—
We turn back to our dying.

notes.n: The men imagine themselves as **ghosts** returning home: they already feel dead. ‘Drag’ is slow and heavy.
Warm, rich imagery of embers in the hearth; perhaps also a hint of blood.
Home has carried on without them; they have been replaced and forgotten.
notes.w: the innocent mice rejoice: the house is theirs;

notes.n: **Repetition** of ‘closed’: they are shut out of home and civilian life. A symbol of rejection.
notes.w: on us the doors are closed,—

notes.n: The refrain becomes a resigned statement: they accept death. ‘Our dying’ is a possessive, as if it is all they own.
notes.w: We turn back to our dying.

stanzas.label: Stanza 7
lines: Since we believe not otherwise can kind fires burn;
Nor ever suns smile true on child, or field, or fruit.
For God's invincible spring our love is made afraid;
Therefore, not loath, we lie out here; therefore were born,
For love of God seems dying.

notes.n: The difficult stanza: the soldiers try to justify their sacrifice: they suffer so that the ‘kind fires’ of home can keep burning. Convoluted syntax shows how hard it is to believe this.
notes.w: Since we believe not otherwise can kind fires burn;

notes.n: **Tricolon** of what they protect: innocence, nature, plenty.
Even faith and the hope of spring now cause fear: their belief is breaking down.
notes.w: For God's invincible spring our love is made afraid;

notes.n: ‘Not loath’ = not unwilling. Repetition of ‘therefore’ sounds like forced logic.
notes.w: Therefore, not loath, we lie out here;

notes.n: **Loss of faith**: the refrain now says God’s love itself is dying. Owen had been a lay assistant to a vicar and lost faith during the war.
notes.w: For love of God seems dying.

stanzas.label: Stanza 8
lines: Tonight, this frost will fasten on this mud and us,
Shrivelling many hands, and puckering foreheads crisp.
The burying-party, picks and shovels in shaking grasp,
Pause over half-known faces. All their eyes are ice,
But nothing happens.

notes.n: The frost grips the men as it grips the mud: soldiers are treated no differently from the earth. **Alliteration** of ‘f’.
notes.w: this frost will fasten on this mud and us,

notes.n: Graphic physical effects of frostbite; ‘crisp’ makes skin sound like a dead leaf.
notes.w: Shrivelling many hands, and puckering foreheads crisp.

notes.n: The burying party recognise comrades only partly: faces disfigured by frost; friendships destroyed.
Ambiguous: the dead men’s eyes frozen, or the living men numb and emotionless. Bleak image of total coldness.
**Cyclical structure**: the poem ends where it began. Even mass death changes nothing: the ultimate **futility**.

summary: Exposure (written 1917–18, published 1920) is Wilfred Owen’s eight-stanza account of soldiers freezing in the trenches while ‘nothing happens’; compare how it presents nature as the real enemy, the futility and boredom of war, suffering and loss of faith, with Owen’s first-hand context.

Repeated line; here a short half-line that changes.
Giving human qualities to nature (merciless winds, fingering snow).
The poem ends where it began, suggesting no progress.
